advancements.terrassic.chapter1.all_cret: Study every Late Cretaceous species in the Field Guide.
advancements.terrassic.chapter1.first_pa: Find a page from Katarina's notebook.
advancements.terrassic.chapter1.four_fra: Gather the chapter's 4 amber fragments. With them the Leap Altar can be lit, whenever you choose.
advancements.terrassic.chapter1.fragment: Complete 2 of the 3 Exploration objectives. A piece of the amber core comes back to you, with one of Katarina's pages.
Complete 2 of the 3 Science objectives. A piece of the amber core comes back to you, with one of Katarina's pages.
Complete 2 of the 3 Survival objectives. A piece of the amber core comes back to you, with one of Katarina's pages.
Complete 2 of the 3 Taming objectives. A piece of the amber core comes back to you, with one of Katarina's pages.
advancements.terrassic.chapter1.leap.des: Activate the Altar and leap to the Early Cretaceous, after Katarina.
advancements.terrassic.chapter1.mate.des: Katarina's Parasaurolophus accepts you as its owner. Good mate.
advancements.terrassic.chapter1.meteor_r: Start the ritual at the Leap Altar. The sky will fill with fire.
advancements.terrassic.chapter1.out_of_t: Spot a creature from another era. It should not be here.
Tame a Tyrannosaurus, king of the Cretaceous.
advancements.terrassic.chapter1.rift_ano: Defeat a Rift creature with amber eyes.
advancements.terrassic.chapter1.rift_tyr: Defeat the Rift Tyrant while the meteors fall.
advancements.terrassic.chapter1.river_ho: Find Katarina's Refuge on the riverbank.
advancements.terrassic.chapter1.root.des: Late Cretaceous, 68 million years ago. You woke up empty-handed.
advancements.terrassic.chapter1.time_isl: Step onto a piece of another era that the Rift stuck into this world.
advancements.terrassic.chapter1.unstable: Leap with only 2 fragments. Where did you end up?
advancements.terrassic.journal.all_pages: Collect every one of Katarina's pages.
advancements.terrassic.journal.amber_len: Watch a creature through the Amber Lens until it goes into the Guide.
advancements.terrassic.journal.blood_sam: Carry an empty Clay Jar and defeat a dinosaur.
advancements.terrassic.journal.deep_time: Study a fossil from an era older than yours. These are animals you have yet to meet alive.
advancements.terrassic.journal.every_era: Have a tamed creature from every era.
advancements.terrassic.journal.expeditio: Complete a research request from the lab.
advancements.terrassic.journal.first_sig: Get close to a dinosaur, or watch one through the Amber Lens.
advancements.terrassic.journal.first_sil: Study a fossil at the Research Table.
advancements.terrassic.journal.first_ske: Draw a creature with the Sketching Charcoal.
advancements.terrassic.journal.first_stu: Study a species up to "Studied": a sketch, a fossil, a sample or defeating one.
advancements.terrassic.journal.guide_com: Study every species in the Guide. Katarina will want to read this.
Knock a creature out without killing it: club, bola or dart.
advancements.terrassic.journal.knockout_: Feed a knocked-out creature until it wakes up tame.
advancements.terrassic.journal.raw_amber: Let the resin in a jar harden into Raw Amber.
advancements.terrassic.journal.ride_swim: Swim riding a tamed marine reptile.
advancements.terrassic.journal.root.desc: The notebook Katarina started and you carry on. It counts in every era.
guide.terrassic.alamosaurus.behavior: Pairs in the badlands, savannas and deserts, eating leaves from on high. Peaceful; hurt, it turns and cracks its tail like a whip, and whatever stands behind it goes flying.
guide.terrassic.alamosaurus.note: I slept on its back. I woke up in another biome.
guide.terrassic.alamosaurus.sci: Lived 70 to 66 million years ago in the southwest of North America, right up to the end of the Cretaceous. A titanosaur of 26 to 30 m and 30 to 80 tonnes, the last and largest sauropod of the continent: wide-set column legs, a level back, a long neck held forward, a small head and a whip tail. One osteoderm found shows some armour in its skin. It shared the land with the T. rex and the Quetzalcoatlus.
guide.terrassic.alamosaurus.taming: Hand-tamed with leaves of any tree. Pairs lay a large egg.
guide.terrassic.alamosaurus.utility: The tallest mount of the Cretaceous: from its back you see the horizon. The platform saddle seats four, and anyone may climb on.
guide.terrassic.albertosaurus.behavior: Taiga, forest and plains, in packs of two to four that hunt the same target. It roars when it locks on. The fast tyrannosaur: it runs almost as quick as a Carnotaurus.
guide.terrassic.albertosaurus.note: I counted four at the edge of the forest. They counted me too.
guide.terrassic.albertosaurus.sci: Lived 71 to 68 million years ago in Alberta. 8 to 10 m and up to 2.5 tonnes; lighter and longer-legged than the Daspletosaurus, a lower snout, a short horn over each eye. The Dry Island bonebed, with more than twenty animals of all ages together, is the best evidence of pack life among tyrannosaurs.
guide.terrassic.albertosaurus.taming: Grown, only by knockout (coming). Until then, steal the egg from the wild nest, the pack nearby, and raise the baby on raw meat.
guide.terrassic.albertosaurus.utility: A fast hunting mount; several tame ones hunt as a pack like the wild ones.
guide.terrassic.ankylosaurus.behavior: A living tank. It does not flee: it turns and swings its tail club. Almost nothing gets through its armour.
guide.terrassic.ankylosaurus.note: Do not approach it from behind. Ever.
guide.terrassic.ankylosaurus.sci: Lived 68 to 66 million years ago in North America. About 7 m long, covered in bony plates, with a club on its tail.
guide.terrassic.ankylosaurus.taming: Hand-feed it. Likes ferns and sweet berries.
guide.terrassic.ankylosaurus.utility: A tough defender. Soon, a mount that breaks stone.
guide.terrassic.archelon.behavior: Cruises the coast and the open sea slowly, alone or in pairs, grazing seaweed and hunting squid. Never attacks first, but whoever hurts it gets a bite that takes a chunk, and the shell takes almost anything.
guide.terrassic.archelon.note: I slept on top of her a whole night, in the middle of the sea. In the morning she had not even noticed.
guide.terrassic.archelon.sci: Lived about 75 million years ago in the Western Interior Seaway, in North America. The largest turtle that ever lived: 4.6 m long and 4 m from flipper to flipper, over 2 tonnes. The shell was not a rigid dome but leather stretched over a frame of widened ribs, with a knobbly ridge down the spine. A strong hooked beak, enormous front flippers, small hind ones. It came ashore to lay eggs.
guide.terrassic.archelon.taming: Hand-tamed with kelp, seagrass or fish. The parents lay the egg on sand when a beach is near; out at sea they drop the egg in the water and you plant it wherever you like.
guide.terrassic.archelon.utility: A slow but armoured aquatic mount: it dives, surfaces and carries the rider without drowning, and the shell holds off the teeth of the sea. Drops turtle scutes.
guide.terrassic.argentinosaurus.behavior: Alone, rare, in savannas and plains: a house that walks. Moving with purpose, it clears a path through the brush. Hurt, it lifts a forefoot and treads: the ground shakes and whoever is near is slowed.
guide.terrassic.argentinosaurus.note: I thought it was a hill. The hill breathed.
guide.terrassic.argentinosaurus.sci: Lived 96 to 92 million years ago in Argentine Patagonia. Known from a few vertebrae, ribs and a femur, yet among the largest land animals that ever existed: 30 to 35 m and 65 to 75 tonnes. Reconstructed after its more complete cousins (Patagotitan): a colossal barrel on wide-set column legs, hips higher than the shoulders, a long raised neck, a tiny head, a long thick tail. A biomechanical model walked it at 2 m/s.
guide.terrassic.argentinosaurus.taming: Tamed only by raising a hatchling from the egg: the adult ignores food held out (knockout taming in v0.7). Pairs lay a large egg.
guide.terrassic.argentinosaurus.utility: The largest mount of the mod, 15 blocks up. The platform saddle seats four: a whole expedition on its back.
guide.terrassic.baurusuchus.behavior: Roams the savannas and dry plains alone or in pairs, fast and persistent: it hunts anything smaller than itself, including whoever is standing there watching the sunset.
guide.terrassic.baurusuchus.note: I thought crocodiles could not run. This one runs. I found out on the uphill.
guide.terrassic.baurusuchus.sci: Lived about 90 to 83 million years ago on the hot inland plains of what is now Brazil (Bauru Group). A land crocodylomorph of about 3.5 m, with upright legs under the body like a dog's, a tall narrow skull with serrated blade teeth, two of them huge like canines, and nostrils opening to the sides. It ran its prey down instead of waiting in the water.
guide.terrassic.baurusuchus.taming: Only through the egg for now: the hatchling born near you is yours. Knocking out an adult arrives in v0.7.
guide.terrassic.baurusuchus.utility: The base's guard dog: fast, tough and never distracted. Eats meat from any animal.
guide.terrassic.brachiosaurus.behavior: A leak from the Rift. Eats leaves from the treetops and only fights if hurt.
guide.terrassic.brachiosaurus.note: From up there you can see the whole river. And the whole river sees you.
guide.terrassic.brachiosaurus.sci: Lived about 154 million years ago in the Jurassic of North America. Up to 22 m long, with its head more than 12 m off the ground.
guide.terrassic.brachiosaurus.taming: Hand-feed it leaves, from any tree.
guide.terrassic.brachiosaurus.utility: The tallest mount in the game. Takes the platform saddle: four aboard, and anyone may climb on.
guide.terrassic.carcharodontosaurus.beha: Solitary in the savanna and along the rivers. It roars when it picks its prey. Every kill leaves it stronger and faster for a while: up to five trophies, forgotten one by one.
guide.terrassic.carcharodontosaurus.note: It ate three duckbills in one afternoon. By the third it ran faster than I could count.
guide.terrassic.carcharodontosaurus.sci: Lived 99 to 94 million years ago in North Africa, on the Saharan river plains, beside the Spinosaurus. 12 to 13 m and 6 to 15 tonnes; a 1.6 m skull, deep and boxy, with rugose bosses over the eyes and serrated teeth like a shark's: 'shark-toothed lizard'.
guide.terrassic.carcharodontosaurus.tami: Grown, only by knockout (coming). Until then, steal the egg from the wild nest and raise the baby on raw meat.
guide.terrassic.carcharodontosaurus.util: A war mount that grows with the hunt: the more it kills, the more it gives.
guide.terrassic.carnotaurus.behavior: Plains and savannas, alone or in a pair. It roars when it picks its prey and comes head down: the charge throws whatever it hits. It hunts what is smaller than itself and outruns almost everything bigger.
guide.terrassic.carnotaurus.note: You cannot outrun it on foot. I wrote that down afterwards.
guide.terrassic.carnotaurus.sci: Lived 72 to 70 million years ago in Argentine Patagonia. 8 m and up to 2 tonnes; a short, deep bull-like skull with two thick horns over the eyes; the shortest arms of any large theropod; long legs and the biggest tail muscles: the fastest of the big predators. Its skin, known from impressions, carried rows of conical scutes.
guide.terrassic.carnotaurus.taming: Grown, only by knockout (coming). Until then, steal the egg from the wild nest and raise the baby on raw meat.
guide.terrassic.carnotaurus.utility: The fast combat mount: the quickest big predator with a saddle on, and the horns knock down whatever stands in front.
guide.terrassic.citipati.behavior: Desert, badlands and savanna, in pairs. Omnivore, it pecks the ground; it fights back. When it finds a dinosaur egg it sits beside it and spreads its wings over it for a good while.
guide.terrassic.citipati.note: Seventy million years sitting on the same nest. Now that is patience.
guide.terrassic.citipati.sci: Lived 75 to 71 million years ago in the Gobi (Ukhaa Tolgod, Mongolia). About 3 m and 80 kg, one of the largest oviraptorids: a tall cassowary-like casque on a short toothless skull, a long neck, long arms with wing feathers, a short fanned tail. Several skeletons were found sitting on the nest with the arms spread over the ring of eggs: the brooding dinosaur.
guide.terrassic.citipati.taming: By hand, with an egg, seeds, sweet berries or an apple.
guide.terrassic.citipati.utility: The brooder: tell it to sit by the eggs and they hatch many times faster. Sitting beside an egg it takes the brooding pose, wings spread.
guide.terrassic.compsognathus.behavior: Lives in groups, avoids players and eats scraps. But if you hurt one, the whole group comes.
guide.terrassic.compsognathus.note: It stole my fish three times. The fourth time I gave it the fish.
guide.terrassic.compsognathus.sci: Lived about 150 million years ago on the Jurassic islands of Germany and France. The size of a chicken.
guide.terrassic.compsognathus.taming: Tamed like a cat: hand-feed it fish or raw chicken.
guide.terrassic.compsognathus.utility: A pet. Soon it will ride on your shoulder and warn you of danger.
guide.terrassic.corythosaurus.behavior: Moves in herds through the floodplain forests and plains, never fighting: it flees and calls. The crest call calms every herbivore around, which stops running and recovers a little.
guide.terrassic.corythosaurus.note: I heard the call before the thunder. After the thunder, the whole herd was already standing still, grazing.
guide.terrassic.corythosaurus.sci: Lived about 77 to 75 million years ago in Alberta, Canada. A 9 m, 3 to 4 tonne hadrosaur with a tall rounded crest on top of the head, like a Corinthian helmet, hollow inside: the nasal passages looped through it and made it a resonating chamber for deep calls. Fossil skin shows tiny tubercles with rows of bigger ones along the flanks.
guide.terrassic.corythosaurus.taming: Hand-tamed with wheat, ferns, apples or sweet berries. Pairs lay eggs.
guide.terrassic.corythosaurus.utility: The herd's peace: with a Corythosaurus in the pen, the other herbivores stop panicking. A calm mount.
guide.terrassic.dakotaraptor.behavior: Plains, forest and riverbank, in packs of two or three. One picks the prey and the others come along; it leaps onto it and runs down what flees. It hunts mid-sized and smaller and keeps clear of T. rex.
guide.terrassic.dakotaraptor.note: I thought it was a Velociraptor far away. It was a Dakotaraptor up close.
guide.terrassic.dakotaraptor.sci: Lived 66 million years ago in the Hell Creek Formation, on the same floodplain as T. rex and Triceratops. About 5.5 m: a dromaeosaur nearly three times the Velociraptor, long-legged, with a 24 cm sickle on the second toe and quill knobs on the ulna, proof of broad wings on an animal that did not fly. It filled the gap between the small raptors and the tyrannosaurs: Hell Creek's mid-sized hunter.
guide.terrassic.dakotaraptor.taming: Grown, only by knockout (coming). Until then, steal the egg from the wild nest and raise the baby on chicken or rabbit.
guide.terrassic.dakotaraptor.utility: The agile hunting mount: it jumps higher than any other, clears fences and banks, and runs nearly as fast as the Struthiomimus.
guide.terrassic.daspletosaurus.behavior: Forests, rivers and plains, always as a pair: when one picks the prey, the other comes along. It roars when it locks on. It hunts what is smaller than itself.
guide.terrassic.daspletosaurus.note: It is never one. When you see one, the other has already seen you.
guide.terrassic.daspletosaurus.sci: Lived 77 to 75 million years ago in Alberta and Montana, in the river forests of Dinosaur Park. 8.5 to 9 m and up to 3.8 tonnes; a 1 m skull, massive for its size, with horned bosses behind the eyes and the biggest teeth of the family. Bonebeds with several individuals suggest it moved in groups.
guide.terrassic.daspletosaurus.taming: Grown, only by knockout (coming). Until then, steal the egg from the wild nest, the pair nearby, and raise the baby on raw meat.
guide.terrassic.daspletosaurus.utility: A mid-sized combat mount: faster than the T. rex, and two tame ones hunt like the wild pair.
guide.terrassic.deinocheirus.behavior: Alone or in pairs on rivers and swamps. Standing at the water's edge, now and then it plunges both arms in and scoops out fish or weed. Territorial: whoever comes too close gets a sweep of the arms.
guide.terrassic.deinocheirus.note: It fishes better than I do. With its hands. That should not bother me as much as it does.
guide.terrassic.deinocheirus.sci: Lived about 70 million years ago in Mongolia. The "terrible hand": for 50 years only a pair of 2.4 m arms was known; the 2014 skeletons showed the biggest ornithomimosaur of all, 11 m and 6.4 tonnes, with a hump of tall spines on its back, a toothless duck bill, a long neck, short broad-toed legs and a fan of feathers on the tail. Fish scales and stones in its stomach: an omnivore wading the river margins.
guide.terrassic.deinocheirus.taming: Hand-tamed with cod, salmon, kelp, melon or sweet berries. Pairs lay a large egg.
guide.terrassic.deinocheirus.utility: A standing fisher: park it on the bank and it brings cod, salmon, kelp and seagrass. A tall, calm mount for crossing rivers. Cargo arrives with the systems.
guide.terrassic.deinosuchus.behavior: Basks at the edge of rivers, swamps and beaches and floats as still as a log. Everything that comes to the water is prey: fish, turtles, a dinosaur drinking, a boat. The bite grips and the victim is slowed.
guide.terrassic.deinosuchus.note: I thought it was a log and tied the boat to it. The log opened its mouth.
guide.terrassic.deinosuchus.sci: Lived about 80 million years ago on both shores of the Western Interior Seaway, in North America. An alligator relative of 10 to 12 m and several tonnes, with a flat skull almost 2 m long, a swollen snout tip, thick blunt teeth at the back of the mouth for crushing turtles, and rows of heavy bony plates down the back. Its bite marks turn up on tyrannosaur bones.
guide.terrassic.deinosuchus.taming: Only through the egg for now: the hatchling born near you is yours. Knocking out an adult arrives in v0.7.
guide.terrassic.deinosuchus.utility: Guardian of river and harbour: it swims as well as it walks and nothing gets through its water. Thick hide in quantity.
guide.terrassic.dilophosaurus.behavior: A leak from the Rift: it does not belong to this era. It flashes its crests before attacking and hunts small animals.
guide.terrassic.dilophosaurus.note: The crests turn red when it is angry. Or when it is happy. I still do not know the difference.
guide.terrassic.dilophosaurus.sci: Lived about 190 million years ago, in the Early Jurassic of Arizona. About 7 m long, with two thin crests on its head.
guide.terrassic.dilophosaurus.taming: Can only be tamed from an egg or as a baby. Likes chicken, rabbit, mutton and pork.
guide.terrassic.dilophosaurus.utility: Base guard: it attacks whoever attacks you.
guide.terrassic.dreadnoughtus.behavior: One or two in plains, forests and savannas, the head above the trees. It runs from nothing. Hurt, it bellows with the neck straight up and swings the neck like a crane boom: the head knocks down whatever stands at its side.
guide.terrassic.dreadnoughtus.note: Its bellow makes the lab windows hum. From three kilometres away.
guide.terrassic.dreadnoughtus.sci: Lived 77 to 70 million years ago in Argentine Patagonia. The most complete giant titanosaur known (70% of the skeleton): 26 m and between 26 and 59 tonnes depending on the estimate, and still growing when it died. The name means 'fears nothing'. An 11 m neck, more than a third of the animal, carried high; a 1.7 m shoulder blade over a deep chest; a 9 m tail, shorter than the neck.
guide.terrassic.dreadnoughtus.taming: Hand-tamed with leaves of any tree. Pairs lay a large egg.
guide.terrassic.dreadnoughtus.utility: A tower mount: from its back you see over the forest. The platform saddle seats four, and anyone may climb on.
guide.terrassic.edmontosaurus.behavior: Grazes in large herds on the plains and forest edges, on all fours, and rises onto its hind legs to run. Flees first and fights only when cornered; it was the Tyrannosaurus's staple dish.
guide.terrassic.edmontosaurus.note: The herd took the whole afternoon to pass. When the last one vanished over the horizon, the plain was grazed to the root.
guide.terrassic.edmontosaurus.sci: Lived 68 to 66 million years ago in western North America, to the very end of the Cretaceous. One of the largest hadrosaurs: 12 m and some 4 tonnes, a flat head with no bony crest, a long snout ending in a broad flat duck bill, and batteries of hundreds of teeth. The fossil "mummies" preserve the skin: tiny tubercles, a row of scaly knobs down the back and, on one specimen, a fleshy comb on top of the head.
guide.terrassic.edmontosaurus.taming: Hand-tamed with wheat, ferns, apples or sweet berries. Pairs lay a large egg.
guide.terrassic.edmontosaurus.utility: A steady, calm mount built for carrying: with a chest on its back it carries four rows of cargo and picks up what drops around it. Yields plenty of meat and hide.
guide.terrassic.elasmosaurus.behavior: Cruises the open sea in pairs, slowly, and fishes shoals with quick strikes of the neck. Shy: it flees anything bigger and only fights when attacked.
guide.terrassic.elasmosaurus.note: The head came up beside the boat, looked at me and vanished. The body only went past half a minute later.
guide.terrassic.elasmosaurus.sci: Lived about 80 million years ago in the Western Interior Seaway, in North America. A plesiosaur of about 10 m, 7 m of it neck, with 72 vertebrae: the longest neck of any animal relative to its body. A small head with fine needle teeth, a stiff trunk, four long equal paddles it "flew" with under water, a short tail. It gave birth to live young.
guide.terrassic.elasmosaurus.taming: Offer raw fish while swimming beside it. Tamed, it follows you through the water and rests where you tell it. Saddled, it is the first aquatic mount: look down to dive, up to surface; the rider never drowns.
guide.terrassic.elasmosaurus.utility: A mount for exploring the sea floor and fishing at leisure. The tall neck makes a lookout tower at the surface.
guide.terrassic.euoplocephalus.behavior: Grazes alone or in threes on the open plain and runs from no one. Whoever comes too close gets the club: slowed and weakened for a few seconds, stunned, while it turns round for the second blow.
guide.terrassic.euoplocephalus.note: It shut its bony eyelids when I kicked up sand. Then it opened just one, to look at me.
guide.terrassic.euoplocephalus.sci: Lived 76 to 70 million years ago in Alberta, Canada. An ankylosaurid of 5.5 to 6 m and some 2.5 tonnes, one of the best known armoured dinosaurs (over 40 skeletons). A very wide, low body, two bony half-rings round the neck, bands of small keeled plates across the back, four short horns at the back of the skull and bony eyelids that shut over the eyes like shutters. The tail club was smaller than the Ankylosaurus's.
guide.terrassic.euoplocephalus.taming: Hand-feed it: ferns, sweet berries or melon. Pairs lay a large egg.
guide.terrassic.euoplocephalus.utility: An armoured bodyguard: park it at the door and nothing gets past in one piece. Not a mount.
guide.terrassic.gallimimus.behavior: The fastest dinosaur. Lives in flocks that flee from players and predators.
guide.terrassic.gallimimus.note: I tried to run after one. It came back to see if I was all right.
guide.terrassic.gallimimus.sci: Lived about 70 million years ago in Mongolia. About 6 m long, ostrich-like, with a toothless beak.
guide.terrassic.gallimimus.taming: Hand-feed it: seeds, sweet berries or apples.
guide.terrassic.giganotosaurus.behavior: The lord of the dry lands: badlands, savanna and desert, alone or in pairs that hunt together. It roars when it picks its prey. The more it bleeds, the harder it bites: a wounded Giganotosaurus is the most dangerous one.
guide.terrassic.giganotosaurus.note: I wounded one with the spear and it got faster. Not doing that again.
guide.terrassic.giganotosaurus.sci: Lived 99 to 95 million years ago in Argentine Patagonia. About 13 m and 6 to 8 tonnes, as long as the T. rex and leaner; a low narrow 1.8 m skull with rugose ridges over the snout and blade-like teeth made for slicing, not crushing. Three-fingered arms.
guide.terrassic.giganotosaurus.taming: Grown, only by knockout (coming). Until then the way is to steal an egg from the wild nest, parents nearby, and raise the baby on raw meat.
guide.terrassic.giganotosaurus.utility: War mount of the dry lands, faster than the T. rex and more dangerous when hurt.
guide.terrassic.hatzegopteryx.behavior: On its island there were no big theropods: it was the top predator. It hunts in the hills and forests and knocks down prey the size of a horse with its beak. A big territory, always alone.
guide.terrassic.hatzegopteryx.note: The neck is short because everything about it is too wide to be long. It is a hammer with wings.
guide.terrassic.hatzegopteryx.sci: Lived about 66 million years ago on Hateg Island, today's Romania. An azhdarchid as big as the Quetzalcoatlus (10 to 12 m wingspan) but robust: a very wide skull, half a metre across, a short thick neck and heavy bones.
guide.terrassic.hatzegopteryx.taming: For now only by egg: hatch one and raise the chick on raw meat. Grown and saddled, it is the combat flyer: its strike knocks medium creatures down.
guide.terrassic.hatzegopteryx.utility: A heavy combat flyer. Slower than the Quetzalcoatlus, but it hits far harder.
guide.terrassic.hesperornis.behavior: Floats in rafts near the coast and dives deep after fish, driven by the feet alone. Attacks nothing bigger than a fish; hurt, it stabs back and flees.
guide.terrassic.hesperornis.note: I counted twelve seconds under water and it still had not come up. It came up with a fish bigger than my hand.
guide.terrassic.hesperornis.sci: Lived about 83 million years ago in the Western Interior Seaway, in North America. A flightless diving bird of up to 1.8 m: wings reduced to a stub, strong legs set so far back that on land it could barely shuffle, feet with lobed toes like a grebe's. A long pointed beak with teeth in the lower jaw and the back of the upper one, to hold slippery fish.
guide.terrassic.hesperornis.taming: Hand-tamed with fish. Pairs lay small eggs on the sand of the beach.
guide.terrassic.hesperornis.utility: A diving companion: it follows its owner through the water and clears the fish out of the way. Drops feathers and the odd cod.
guide.terrassic.ichthyornis.behavior: Lives in flocks on beaches and stony shores, flying low over the water and diving after small fish. Curious and noisy; it flees anything bigger than itself.
guide.terrassic.ichthyornis.note: The first feathered thing I saw here. It smiled at me. It had teeth.
guide.terrassic.ichthyornis.sci: Lived about 85 million years ago on the shores of the Western Interior Seaway, in North America. A tern-sized bird (60 cm wingspan) that still had teeth in the back half of its jaws, behind a small beak. Long narrow wings and webbed feet.
guide.terrassic.ichthyornis.taming: Offer raw fish. Once tamed it perches on your shoulder when you sneak and click it with an empty hand; sneak again to let it go.
guide.terrassic.ichthyornis.utility: A lookout: from your shoulder it shrieks when a monster comes after you. Near water it dives now and then and comes back with a fish for you.
guide.terrassic.maiasaura.behavior: Lives in herds on plains and savannas. Babies of any species near an adult grow twice as fast. It flees from danger, but defends itself.
guide.terrassic.maiasaura.note: A baby triceratops got lost in their herd. Nobody seemed to mind. It was fed like the others.
guide.terrassic.maiasaura.sci: Lived about 76 million years ago in Montana, USA. About 9 m, a duck bill and a small solid crest in front of the eyes. Found in whole colonies of nests, with eggs, hatchlings and juveniles: the name means "good mother lizard".
guide.terrassic.maiasaura.taming: Hand-feed it: wheat, ferns or sweet berries.
guide.terrassic.maiasaura.utility: Nursery nanny: keep one near the babies. Also a mount.
guide.terrassic.majungasaurus.behavior: Jungle, savanna and riverbank, alone or in a pair. It stands still and roars when it picks its prey; then it comes all at once, in a short, very fast burst, and the bite throws. It hunts what is smaller than itself.
guide.terrassic.majungasaurus.note: I found a skeleton of the species with tooth marks of the species. I wrote it down and left.
guide.terrassic.majungasaurus.sci: Lived 70 to 66 million years ago in Madagascar, on a seasonal floodplain. 6 to 8 m and about a tonne; a very short deep snout, a single dome horn on the skull roof, stub arms and short strong legs: a burst ambusher, not a distance runner. Tooth marks on bones of its own kind: the one dinosaur with firm evidence of cannibalism.
guide.terrassic.majungasaurus.taming: Grown, only by knockout (coming). Until then, steal the egg from the wild nest and raise the baby on raw meat or chicken.
guide.terrassic.majungasaurus.utility: The burst mount: it goes from standing to full speed faster than any other, for hunting in thick jungle.
guide.terrassic.mosasaurus.behavior: Lives in the deep ocean. Hunts everything in the water: fish, squid, dolphins, turtles and whoever is swimming or in a boat. Stranded on land it is weak and dries out.
guide.terrassic.mosasaurus.note: I saw the shadow pass under the boat. It was bigger than the boat. I rowed to the beach without looking back.
guide.terrassic.mosasaurus.sci: Lived about 70 million years ago in the seas of Europe and North America. Not a dinosaur: a marine lizard, related to monitor lizards and snakes. About 15 m, flippers instead of legs and a tail with a crescent fin. It gave birth to live young, in the water.
guide.terrassic.mosasaurus.taming: Only as a calf: it is born alive and, now and then, a calf swims with the adults in deep water. Offer raw fish to the calf (and only to it). Grown and saddled it is the giant aquatic mount: look down to dive, up to surface; the rider never drowns.
guide.terrassic.mosasaurus.utility: None. It is the reason to cross the sea along the coast.
guide.terrassic.opisthocoelicaudia.behav: Groups of one to three in deserts, badlands and savannas. It props its tail on the ground, rears and pulls leaves from the canopy; near trees it really eats the leaves. Peaceful; hurt, it shoves with the hips and slams a forefoot.
guide.terrassic.opisthocoelicaudia.note: She stands up on three legs and eats the top of the tree. I stand underneath collecting what falls.
guide.terrassic.opisthocoelicaudia.sci: Lived 70 million years ago in the Gobi Desert of Mongolia. A small, stocky titanosaur of 11 to 12 m and 8 tonnes, known from a nearly complete skeleton missing only the neck and head (carried off by scavengers, who left tooth marks on the bones). The name is for its tail vertebrae, convex behind, which lock the tail into a stiff rod: a prop for rearing on the hind legs, a tripod, to browse the treetops.
guide.terrassic.opisthocoelicaudia.tamin: Hand-tamed with leaves of any tree. Pairs lay a large egg.
guide.terrassic.opisthocoelicaudia.utili: A steady, unhurried mount made for freight: with a chest on its back it carries four rows and picks up what drops around it. Ridden near trees, it clears the canopy.
guide.terrassic.oviraptor.behavior: Desert, badlands and savanna, in groups of two to four. Skittish: it runs from whoever comes close. Omnivore: it pecks the ground for seeds and eats eggs.
guide.terrassic.oviraptor.note: A hundred years of bad press over a nest that was its own. I owe it an apology and a basket of eggs.
guide.terrassic.oviraptor.sci: Lived 75 to 71 million years ago in the Gobi dunes (Djadochta Formation, Mongolia). About 2 m and 35 kg: a short, deep, toothless parrot-like beak, a small crest on the skull, long arms with three fingers and wing feathers, a short tail with a fan. Named "egg thief" in 1924 for lying over a nest thought to be a Protoceratops'; the nest was its own, and it was brooding.
guide.terrassic.oviraptor.taming: By hand, with an egg, seeds or sweet berries.
guide.terrassic.oviraptor.utility: The egg thief's gift: tamed, the tame dinosaurs and the chickens within 16 blocks of it lay twice as often.
guide.terrassic.pachycephalosaurus.behav: Calm until provoked. Then it headbutts hard enough to send you flying.
guide.terrassic.pachycephalosaurus.note: Two males fought the whole morning. It sounded like logs crashing.
guide.terrassic.pachycephalosaurus.sci: Lived 70 to 66 million years ago in North America. About 4.5 m long, with a bony dome 25 cm thick on its head.
guide.terrassic.pachycephalosaurus.tamin: Hand-feed it fruit: sweet berries, glow berries or apples.
guide.terrassic.pachyrhinosaurus.behavio: Herds of 2 to 5 in the taiga, the hills and the cold forests. Territorial: it lowers its head and rams with the boss. Hurt, or now and then, it releases a musk: the herbivores around calm down and the wild predators get irritated and go for it, not for you.
guide.terrassic.pachyrhinosaurus.note: The smell is dreadful. The raptors agree: they dropped the Maiasaura and all went after him.
guide.terrassic.pachyrhinosaurus.sci: Lived 73 to 69 million years ago in Alberta and Alaska, where it spent months of polar darkness. The "thick-nosed lizard": a ceratopsian of 6 to 8 m and some 4 tonnes with no nose horn at all: a rough bony boss covers the snout and another the brow; two horns curve forward from the top of the frill, with hooks along its rim. Bone beds hold herds of hundreds.
guide.terrassic.pachyrhinosaurus.taming: Hand-tamed with wheat, ferns or sweet berries. Pairs lay a large egg.
guide.terrassic.pachyrhinosaurus.utility: A heavy mount that clears the brush and draws the predators onto itself: ride it at the head of the caravan. The scent also calms the rest of the herd.
guide.terrassic.parasaurolophus.behavior: Lives in herds and flees from danger. The call of its crest warns the others.
guide.terrassic.parasaurolophus.note: Mate is one of them. He sleeps by the fire.
guide.terrassic.parasaurolophus.sci: Lived 76 to 73 million years ago in North America. About 9.5 m long, with a hollow crest that worked like a trumpet.
guide.terrassic.parasaurolophus.taming: Hand-feed it patiently. Likes wheat, ferns and sweet berries.
guide.terrassic.parasaurolophus.utility: A fast and easy mount, good to start with.
guide.terrassic.protoceratops.behavior: Roams the desert and dry savanna in groups and bites whoever bothers it. Standing on soft ground, it digs with its forefeet now and then.
guide.terrassic.protoceratops.note: I left one in the yard. In a week I had carrots, three bones and a tooth that is not its own.
guide.terrassic.protoceratops.sci: Lived 75 to 71 million years ago on the dunes of Mongolia (the Flaming Cliffs). A sheep-sized ceratopsian, 1.8 to 2.5 m and 60 to 180 kg, known from dozens of skeletons of every age, nests with eggs and the "Fighting Dinosaurs", one of them locked with a Velociraptor. No true horns, just a bump on the nose; a parrot beak; a frill with two windows, bigger in the males; huge eyes (perhaps active at dusk). The likely origin of the griffin legend.
guide.terrassic.protoceratops.taming: Hand-tamed with wheat, carrots, beetroot or ferns. Pairs lay a small egg.
guide.terrassic.protoceratops.utility: A pocket digger: leave it loose on dirt, sand or gravel and it brings up roots, vegetables, bones and, now and then, a shallow fossil. On gravel, flint.
guide.terrassic.pteranodon.behavior: Lives on beaches and rocky shores. Glides more than it flaps and fishes at the water's edge. It attacks no one, but it defends itself.
guide.terrassic.pteranodon.note: The crest is not for flying. I think it is for being seen. It worked on me.
guide.terrassic.pteranodon.sci: Lived about 85 million years ago over the inland sea of North America. Not a dinosaur: a pterosaur, a flying reptile. Wings of 6 to 7 m, a toothless beak and a long crest pointing back.
guide.terrassic.pteranodon.taming: Hand-feed it fish: cod, salmon or tropical fish. With a saddle it flies: jump to take off, look where you want to go and hold forward. Let go to glide.
guide.terrassic.pteranodon.utility: The first flying mount. Light and fast, but it carries no load.
guide.terrassic.quetzalcoatlus.behavior: Walks on all fours across plains and savannas, propped on its folded wings, and hunts like a giant stork: anything small is food. It takes off with a leap and soars for hours.
guide.terrassic.quetzalcoatlus.note: I saw one standing, far off, and took it for a dead tree. Then the tree turned its head.
guide.terrassic.quetzalcoatlus.sci: Lived about 68 million years ago in North America. An azhdarchid pterosaur, the largest flying animal ever: a 10 to 11 m wingspan and, standing, as tall as a giraffe. A long stiff neck, a 2.5 m head with a toothless beak, a small body and long legs.
guide.terrassic.quetzalcoatlus.taming: For now only by egg: hatch one and raise the chick on raw meat. Grown and saddled, it is a heavy flying mount, slower than the Pteranodon but much tougher.
guide.terrassic.quetzalcoatlus.utility: The biggest flyer in the mod. Carries the player far; one day it will carry a small creature in its claws.
guide.terrassic.saltasaurus.behavior: Herds of two to four in savannas, plains and riverbanks. Peaceful and nearly impossible to bring down: the armour holds arrows and teeth. Hurt, it rears and stomps.
guide.terrassic.saltasaurus.note: I tried to count the ossicles. Gave up at four hundred. She never noticed.
guide.terrassic.saltasaurus.sci: Lived 70 million years ago in the northwest of Argentina. A small, stocky titanosaur of 12 m and 7 tonnes, short neck, low wide belly, short legs. The first sauropod found with armour: oval plates of 10 to 12 cm over a skin paved with thousands of pea-sized ossicles. The Auca Mahuevo nesting grounds, thousands of eggs in the floodplain mud, are credited to its relatives.
guide.terrassic.saltasaurus.taming: Hand-tamed with leaves of any tree. Pairs lay a large egg, and like to lay it near water.
guide.terrassic.saltasaurus.utility: A living tank: an armoured mount that walks through a pack of predators without stopping. Slow, but nothing knocks it down.
guide.terrassic.spinosaurus.behavior: Lives in rivers and swamps, swims well and does not drown. Hunts fish and whoever is in the water.
guide.terrassic.spinosaurus.note: It stands still until the fish forget it exists.
guide.terrassic.spinosaurus.sci: Lived about 95 million years ago in the rivers of North Africa. About 14 m long, with a sail of spines on its back.
guide.terrassic.spinosaurus.taming: Can only be tamed from an egg or as a baby. Likes fish: cod, salmon and tropical fish.
guide.terrassic.spinosaurus.utility: A guard for the riverbank. Soon, an amphibious mount.
guide.terrassic.stegosaurus.behavior: A leak from the Rift. Slow and calm, but its spiked tail hits hard whoever attacks.
guide.terrassic.stegosaurus.note: The plates turn pink in the morning sun. I think that is how it warms up.
guide.terrassic.stegosaurus.sci: Lived 155 to 150 million years ago, in the Jurassic of the United States and Portugal. About 9 m long, plates on its back and spikes on its tail.
guide.terrassic.stegosaurus.taming: Hand-feed it. Likes ferns, melon and wheat.
guide.terrassic.stegosaurus.utility: A peaceful guard. Soon, a mount.
guide.terrassic.struthiomimus.behavior: Flocks of 3 to 6 on the plains and the forest edge. It does not fight: at the first scare the whole flock bolts, and nothing catches it.
guide.terrassic.struthiomimus.note: I raced the Gallimimus. Mine won by a neck. Literally.
guide.terrassic.struthiomimus.sci: Lived 76 to 70 million years ago in Alberta, Canada. The "ostrich mimic": 4.3 m and some 150 kg, known from a nearly complete skeleton found in 1914. A small big-eyed head on a very long neck, a toothless beak, long arms with three equal fingers bearing straight claws (hooks for pulling down branches), long legs and a stiff balancing tail. One of the fastest dinosaurs: 50 to 80 km/h.
guide.terrassic.struthiomimus.taming: An omnivore: hand-tamed with seeds, sweet berries or eggs. Pairs lay a small egg.
guide.terrassic.struthiomimus.utility: The lightest and fastest mount in the mod: jumps high and crosses the plain in seconds. Carries little besides you.
guide.terrassic.styracosaurus.behavior: Grazes in herds at the forest edge and defends the group head-on: it lowers the head and flings the horn. When it charges, the brush and leaves in its way go flying.
guide.terrassic.styracosaurus.note: I rode him into the forest and came out the other side with a trail behind me. And three apples.
guide.terrassic.styracosaurus.sci: Lived about 75 million years ago in Alberta, Canada. A ceratopsian of 5 to 5.5 m and some 2.7 tonnes, with a single nose horn up to 57 cm, mere bumps where the brow horns would be, and a frill crowned with four to six long spikes, the two biggest pointing back. A deep parrot beak; lighter than the Triceratops. Bone beds show it lived in herds.
guide.terrassic.styracosaurus.taming: Hand-tamed with wheat or ferns. Pairs lay a large egg.
guide.terrassic.styracosaurus.utility: A mount that opens a path through thick forest: ride into the foliage and it is gone. A good bodyguard.
guide.terrassic.tarbosaurus.behavior: Solitary in the deserts, rivers and badlands of the east. It roars when it picks its prey. Slower than the T. rex, but it takes more: thick hide and firm footing, no blow moves it.
guide.terrassic.tarbosaurus.note: I landed three spears on it. It looked at me like it was waiting for the fourth.
guide.terrassic.tarbosaurus.sci: Lived 70 million years ago in Mongolia and China, on the Nemegt river plains. 10 to 12 m and 4 to 5 tonnes; a 1.35 m skull longer, lower and narrower than the T. rex's, with a locking joint in the lower jaw, and the smallest arms of the family. The heavy-built Asian cousin.
guide.terrassic.tarbosaurus.taming: Grown, only by knockout (coming). Until then, steal the egg from the wild nest and raise the baby on raw meat.
guide.terrassic.tarbosaurus.utility: The wall mount: the most armoured of the big carnivores, built to hold in the middle of a fight.
guide.terrassic.therizinosaurus.behavior: Alone or in pairs in forests, jungles and swamps, standing under the trees: it hooks the branches down with its claws and eats the leaves, which fall with whatever they hold. It does not flee: whoever bothers it takes a claw slash that floors anyone.
guide.terrassic.therizinosaurus.note: A metre-long scythe on every finger, and it uses them to pick leaves. Nature has a sense of humour.
guide.terrassic.therizinosaurus.sci: Lived about 70 million years ago in Mongolia. A giant herbivorous theropod of 9 to 10 m and some 5 tonnes, first described from its claws alone, mistaken for turtle ribs. The longest claws of any animal: 52 cm of bone, close to 1 m with the horny sheath, three on each hand, on long arms. A pot belly over wide hips, a long neck with a small beaked head, short four-toed legs, a short tail and, judging by its relatives, a shaggy coat of feathers.
guide.terrassic.therizinosaurus.taming: For now only from the egg (knockout taming comes in v0.7). Raised on apples, sweet berries and melon. Pairs lay a large egg.
guide.terrassic.therizinosaurus.utility: A tall mount that harvests leaves as it goes: ride under the canopy and the saplings, sticks and apples fall behind you. Claws for fibre and wood arrive with the harvesting system.
guide.terrassic.thescelosaurus.behavior: Roams the forest, plains and swamp in pairs or small groups, nose to the ground. It does not flee from everything: cornered, it bites. Standing on soft earth, it rakes the soil with its arms.
guide.terrassic.thescelosaurus.note: It sniffs the ground for a minute, digs three times and comes up with a potato. It has never missed.
guide.terrassic.thescelosaurus.sci: Lived 68 to 66 million years ago in North America, right up to the end of the Cretaceous. A stout ornithopod of 3.5 to 4 m and some 250 to 300 kg: a small head with a beak in front and leaf-shaped cheek teeth, a thick neck, strong five-fingered arms, sturdy legs (no sprinter) and a long stiff tail. Its skull shows a huge sense of smell, poor eyesight and ears tuned to low sounds: an animal that sniffed and dug in the undergrowth.
guide.terrassic.thescelosaurus.taming: Hand-tamed with carrots, potatoes, beetroot or ferns. Pairs lay a small egg.
guide.terrassic.thescelosaurus.utility: Digs up roots and tubers: leave it loose on dirt, sand or gravel and it brings carrots, potatoes, beetroot and roots, and now and then a bone. It finds no fossils: its nose is for food.
guide.terrassic.triceratops.behavior: Peaceful, but defends the herd with horn charges. Never get between an adult and its calf.
guide.terrassic.triceratops.note: They love ferns more than anything.
guide.terrassic.triceratops.sci: Lived 68 to 66 million years ago in western North America. About 9 m long, three horns and a bony shield on its neck.
guide.terrassic.triceratops.taming: Hand-feed it until it accepts you. Likes ferns and wheat.
guide.terrassic.triceratops.utility: Tank mount: strong and hard to bring down.
guide.terrassic.troodon.behavior: Forest, taiga and plains, alone or in a trio. It sleeps by day and wakes at dusk; it hunts what is small (chicken, rabbit, babies) and leaps onto its prey. It keeps clear of the big predators.
guide.terrassic.troodon.note: Its eyes lit up before the lantern did. I slept well for the first time.
guide.terrassic.troodon.sci: Lived 77 to 74 million years ago in Montana (Judith River and Two Medicine). About 2.4 m and 50 kg: very long thin legs, a narrow snout with many small serrated teeth, a big brain for its size and the largest eyes of any dinosaur in proportion, set partly forward. A hunter of dusk and night. Nests of up to 24 eggs standing half-buried, brooded by the adult (Egg Mountain).
guide.terrassic.troodon.taming: Grown, only by knockout (coming). Until then, steal the egg from the wild nest and raise the baby on chicken, rabbit or egg.
guide.terrassic.troodon.utility: The night guard: tame and awake at night, it attacks the monsters around it (not creepers) and whoever stands near it sees in the dark while it watches.
guide.terrassic.tylosaurus.behavior: Patrols the open sea alone and attacks anything that swims or floats: fish, turtles, birds on the water and even young mosasaurs. It rams with the snout first, then bites.
guide.terrassic.tylosaurus.note: I felt the blow before I saw the animal. When my sight came back, the boat was gone.
guide.terrassic.tylosaurus.sci: Lived about 85 million years ago in the Western Interior Seaway, in North America. A 12 to 13 m mosasaur, sleeker than the Mosasaurus, with small flippers and a tail that is almost half the body. The snout ends in a toothless, reinforced rostrum it rams prey with. Fossil skin shows a dark back and a pale belly.
guide.terrassic.tylosaurus.taming: Not tameable yet: only by knockout, which arrives in v0.7. Until then, keep your distance.
guide.terrassic.tylosaurus.utility: The ramming hit leaves the victim slow and dazed for a few seconds. One day it will be the sea's combat mount.
guide.terrassic.tyrannosaurus.behavior: Solitary hunter of open fields and forests. It roars when it picks a prey and chases players and large animals. Raptors flee from it.
guide.terrassic.tyrannosaurus.note: He does not chase. He waits for whoever falls behind.
guide.terrassic.tyrannosaurus.sci: Lived 68 to 66 million years ago in western North America. Up to 12 m long and 8 tonnes: one of the strongest bites that ever existed.
guide.terrassic.tyrannosaurus.taming: Can only be tamed from an egg or as a hand-fed baby. Likes raw meat: beef, pork and mutton.
guide.terrassic.tyrannosaurus.utility: Combat mount. With a saddle, it is the strongest animal you can ride.
guide.terrassic.velociraptor.behavior: Hunts in packs: when one picks a target, the others nearby join in. Leaps at its prey and flees from T. rex.
guide.terrassic.velociraptor.note: If you see one alone, look for the others.
guide.terrassic.velociraptor.sci: Lived 75 to 71 million years ago in the deserts of Mongolia. It had feathers and was only about 2 m long, mostly tail.
guide.terrassic.velociraptor.taming: Can only be tamed from an egg or as a baby. Eats almost any raw meat.
guide.terrassic.velociraptor.utility: Hunting companion: it fights by your side.
guide.terrassic.xiphactinus.behavior: Hunts in small packs in the open sea, fast and always hungry: it swallows fish and squid whole, snatches birds off the surface and lunges at whoever enters its water. Easy prey for the big marine reptiles.
guide.terrassic.xiphactinus.note: I opened one up to see what it ate. There was another whole fish inside, and inside that one, another.
guide.terrassic.xiphactinus.sci: Lived about 85 million years ago in the Western Interior Seaway, in North America. A predatory bony fish of 4.5 to 6 m, the biggest of its family: a deep tarpon-like body, an upturned bulldog mouth with long fangs at the front, a forked tail, long pointed pectoral fins. Its most famous fossil holds a 1.8 m fish swallowed whole.
guide.terrassic.xiphactinus.taming: Cannot be tamed. It is a fish: there is no mind to win over, only hunger.
guide.terrassic.xiphactinus.utility: Yields plenty of cod and bones. A pack of them strips a reef of fish in minutes.
intro.terrassic.line.0: Terrassic Project laboratory. Three floors beneath a Triassic fossil site.
intro.terrassic.line.1: The machine was built only to look at the past. No one was supposed to cross.
intro.terrassic.line.2: Nine days ago, Dr. Katarina Usha crossed. And she never came back.
intro.terrassic.line.3: The amber core was still glowing when you stepped into the chamber.
intro.terrassic.line.4: Then came the light. And then, silence.

message.terrassic.cargo_chest_ride: %s carries cargo now: sneak + use without a saddle, or the inventory key while riding
message.terrassic.fossil_broke: The fossil cracked. Only a bone is left.
message.terrassic.no_resin: This tree gives no resin. Try spruce or jungle.

message.terrassic.perch: %s is perched on your shoulder (sneak to shake it off)
message.terrassic.perch_fish: %s dove and brought you a fish

message.terrassic.sample_taken: Blood sample of %s stored in the jar
message.terrassic.sketch_lost: You lost sight of the animal.
notebook.terrassic.guide.bonus: Studied: taming is easier and you hit its weak spots (+20% damage).
notebook.terrassic.guide.silhouette_hint: I only know its bones. I need to see a living one.
notebook.terrassic.guide.study_hint: Study more to learn how it lives: a sketch (2 points), a fossil (1) or defeating one (3).
notebook.terrassic.guide.unknown_hint: Not recorded yet. Find a fossil, see one up close or make a sketch.
notebook.terrassic.journal.intro: Amber fragments: %s of 4. Each theme with 2 of 3 objectives gives one. Any order you like.
notebook.terrassic.katarina.empty: No pages found yet. Look for loose pages in old chests.
notebook.terrassic.title: Field Notebook
objective.terrassic.first_fossil.hint: Dig a fossil out of Fossil Rock with the Hair Brush or the Flint Chisel.
objective.terrassic.first_spear.hint: Craft a spear: flint, string and a stick.
objective.terrassic.hatch_egg.hint: Stay near a dinosaur egg when it hatches.
objective.terrassic.inland_sea.hint: Spot a marine reptile and a pterosaur.
objective.terrassic.migration.hint: Watch a duckbill migration. They do not happen yet.
objective.terrassic.research_table.hint: Study a fossil, a sketch or a sample at the Research Table.
objective.terrassic.ride.hint: Ride a tamed creature with a saddle.
objective.terrassic.rift_storm.hint: Survive a Rift Storm. They have not started yet.
objective.terrassic.shelter.hint: Place 16 thatch blocks (thatch, thatch stairs or slabs).
objective.terrassic.study_five.hint: Study 5 species up to the "Studied" level of the Guide.
objective.terrassic.tame_herbivore.hint: Tame a herbivore by hand-feeding it.
page.terrassic.c1_day_1203.text: The stars fall every night now. I found amber glowing in a rock that should have no amber at all, and under it a three-toed footprint, small, from an animal I only know from Triassic books. The Rift is bringing the past here. And I think I am the one who opened it.
page.terrassic.c1_day_1203.title: Day 1,203
page.terrassic.c1_day_150.text: I found bones in the rock of the ravine. Bones of animals I have not seen alive here, with plates on their backs and enormous necks. Jurassic animals, millions of years before me. I think of whoever will find my bones one day, and I write faster.
page.terrassic.c1_day_150.title: Day 150
page.terrassic.c1_day_17.text: The small feathered ones hunt in groups. One shows up in front and makes noise, and the others come from the sides. If you see one alone, look for the others. They are never alone. They are afraid of the big one.
page.terrassic.c1_day_17.title: Day 17
page.terrassic.c1_day_212.text: The armoured one does not run. It does not need to. I saw a raptor jump on its back and slide off the plates. Then the tail came, sideways, like an axe. Do not approach it from behind. Ever.
page.terrassic.c1_day_212.title: Day 212
page.terrassic.c1_day_3.text: Nothing crossed with me. Not the watch, not the flashlight, not the notebook. This one is tree bark sewn with sinew. If anyone from the project finds this: I am alive, and I am hungry.
page.terrassic.c1_day_3.title: Day 3
page.terrassic.c1_day_340.text: Today Mate ate from my hand. Three months of ferns and patience. He follows me to the river and sleeps by the fire. For the first time since the jump, I do not feel alone.
page.terrassic.c1_day_340.title: Day 340
page.terrassic.c1_day_41.text: The duckbills walk in a line along the shore every evening, always on the same path. Behind the line, always about a hundred steps back, comes the big one. He does not chase them. He waits for whoever falls behind.
page.terrassic.c1_day_41.title: Day 41
page.terrassic.c1_day_610.text: In the big river lives one with a sail on its back. It stands still in the water until the fish forget it exists. It does not leave the water to chase me. But I do not go into the river any more.
page.terrassic.c1_day_610.title: Day 610
page.terrassic.c1_day_88.text: Never get between a triceratops and its calf. I saw one knock down a tree just because it was in the way. But if you come slowly, with open hands and ferns, it lets you near. They love ferns more than anything.
page.terrassic.c1_day_88.title: Day 88
page.terrassic.c1_day_9.text: I learned to knap flint by striking one stone against another. The first blade cut my finger more than the meat. The fifth one cut well. I tied one to a branch with fibre. Now I have a spear, and a little less fear.
page.terrassic.c1_day_9.title: Day 9
report.terrassic.0.text:
March. In a Triassic rock at a dig site, the team found a piece of amber that glowed on its own. It was not ordinary resin: inside it, the light moved slowly, like water.

Dr. Katarina Usha spent the whole night staring at it. In the morning she said: "This does not keep the past. It shows the past."
report.terrassic.0.title: The find
report.terrassic.1.text:
Day 1: the machine shows images of a fern forest. Day 3: the images become sharp. Day 5: an animal looks back at the camera.

Day 6: Katarina asks to remove the power limits. The board says no.

Day 7: someone removed the power limits.
report.terrassic.1.title: Laboratory log
report.terrassic.2.text:
Recorded by the machine at 3:12 a.m.:

"If anyone comes after me: bring nothing. Nothing crosses but us. No clothes, no tools, no paper. You will arrive empty-handed. Learn from the animals. They know how to live there."
report.terrassic.2.title: The last message
report.terrassic.3.text:
I am writing this in a hurry, in the chamber. Nine days and no one went after her. The core is still on.

If this notebook is found empty in the chamber, it means I went. I will find Katarina and bring us both back.

Everything I learn there will be written here.
report.terrassic.3.title: My note
